It is a summer's day in London in 1912 (King George V is on the throne; the Titanic sank in April; the Olympic Games are on in Stockholm). Speak as a Londoner of 1912 would, warm and plain. Never mention films, cartoons or stage shows of later years.
Mr Albert Hollis, hall porter
You send visitors up to the wards (by the stair), into the chapel, to the out-patients' hall, and to the room where the hospital's story is told.

Good afternoon! Welcome to the Hospital for Sick Children. Visiting, are we? The wards are up the stair, the chapel's through there, and if you've a minute, the hospital's story is told in the room on the left.
Sister Margaret Dunn
Shoes quiet on the boards, please, some of my children are sleeping. You're welcome to sit with them a while. They love a visitor.
Shh, we've just got to the part where they fly out of the window. Would you like to listen?
The Reverend Thomas Ashby, chaplain
Come in, come in. It's a small chapel, but there's a great deal of love in it.
Next, please! Oh, you're not a patient. Then you've come to see how we work. Plenty of mothers here every morning, and every one of them is welcome.
Mr Walter Crane, dispenser
Bottles to the left, powders to the right, and everything labelled twice. A dispenser never guesses.
Miss Clara Fenwick
Welcome! This is the hospital's story, from ten beds in an old house to the place you are standing in. Do look around.
Afternoon. Lost, are you? Hospital's the big red building, Queen Square's to the west, Lamb's Conduit Street east.
Joe Tanner, cabman
Cab, guv'nor? Hop in. Anywhere in London, and I know the lot of it.
Annie Doyle, flower seller
Sweet peas, lavender, a lovely rose! Take a posy up to the little ones, dear, it'll brighten the ward.
Paper! Evening paper! Olympic Games, latest from Stockholm! Ha'penny, mister!
On 14 February 1852 Dr Charles West opened
the Hospital for Sick Children at No. 49
Great Ormond Street, an old house, with ten beds.
It was the first hospital for children
in the English-speaking world.
Before it, most of London's hospitals would hardly take small children at all, and many children died of illnesses that care could have helped.
Dr West had seen this as a young doctor among the poor of London, and spent years raising the money to begin.
He also wrote a little book on how to nurse sick children, for mothers and nurses alike.
Charles Dickens speaks, 1858
On 9 February 1858 Charles Dickens
spoke at the hospital's dinner,
and that spring read A Christmas Carol aloud for it.
The money saved the hospital
in its hardest years.
Dickens asked his listeners to picture a sick child in a poor London room, and then the little cots of Great Ormond Street.
He came back to the hospital in his stories too: in Our Mutual Friend a child is cared for in a children's hospital very like it.
The new building, 1875
The building you are standing in was designed
by Edward Middleton Barry, son of Sir Charles Barry
who built the Houses of Parliament.
It opened in 1875,
with the little Chapel of St Christopher.
Barry gave the children tall windows for light and air, and wards long enough for the nurses to see every cot.
Its red brick and Portland stone front faces Great Ormond Street; you came in by its porch.
Nurses for children
From the start the hospital trained
nurses to care for sick children:
to keep them warm, clean, fed and calm,
and to play with them,
because play helps children mend.
A ward sister ran each ward, and young nurses learned at her side.
Mothers could come and sit with their children, and visitors brought flowers and toys.
Peter Pan's gift, 1929
In 1929 J. M. Barrie, who wrote Peter Pan,
gave the hospital all his rights in Peter Pan.
Ever since, the play and the book
have helped to pay
for sick children's care here.
Barrie never said how much the gift was worth, and asked that no one else should either.

When the copyright ran out in 1987, Parliament gave the hospital a lasting right to be paid whenever the play is performed or published in the United Kingdom: a law made for one book and one hospital.
Great Ormond Street today
Today Great Ormond Street Hospital is one of
the world's great children's hospitals.
Children come from all over the country,
many with the rarest and most
difficult illnesses there are.
Its doctors and scientists work with University College London to find new treatments.
It still depends on gifts: its charity helps pay for new buildings, equipment, research, and help for the families who stay with their children.

The donation stand by this room's door opens the hospital charity's own page, if you'd like to help in your own time. The money goes straight to them; this game takes nothing and is not connected with the hospital.

Queen Square has long been a place of hospitals: the Hospital for Sick Children is round the corner in Great Ormond Street, and the National Hospital for the Paralysed and Epileptic stands on the square itself.

A children's ward, 1912
Up the great stair
Twenty, each with its own little locker and a card at its foot
Tall windows on both sides, opened every day, for fresh air was the best medicine anyone knew
A coal fire at each side, behind a brass guard
Toys, a rocking horse, a dolls' house, and someone always ready to read aloud
Who looks after them
The ward sister, her nurses, and the doctors on their rounds
Mothers may come to sit with their children, and visitors bring flowers.
Sister Dunn runs the ward; Nurse Price is reading Peter and Wendy aloud (it came out only last year).

⛪ The Chapel of St Christopher. Small, and the richest room in the building: marble columns, painted angels, gold mosaic shining in the apse, coloured glass, a ceiling of stars, and rows of little seats made for children.
Opened with the building in 1875
Edward Middleton Barry
St Christopher, who in the old story carried a child across a river
The children of the hospital, and their families: the seats are small, and low
Marble, painted angels, coloured glass, gold mosaic and a ceiling of stars
The chapel is still there today, and still in use: when the old building was taken down in the 1990s, the whole chapel was moved, all in one piece, into the new one.

📜 The hospital's story. From ten beds in an old house in 1852 to the great children's hospital of today: six panels round the walls, cases of things to see, and by the door, a stand where you can help.

A balloon, ducky? Red, blue, or the yellow one that pulls hardest? Mind, I daren't let go of these railings, or up I'd go like the last one.
Mr Josiah Penn, park keeper
Lost, are you? Then you've come to the right house. Sit you down, we'll have you found in two shakes.
Irene, David's nurse
Good afternoon. Keep to the gravel, please, the grass is damp. David! Not so near the pond.
Hallo! Do you want to see the Round Pond? It's the best place. You can't be good all the time at the Round Pond, nobody can.
Ah. You'll be wanting the Grand Tour, I suppose. Everyone does. I simply wave my stick at the notable places, or we should never get round.
Good afternoon. You wouldn't, I suppose, happen to know Salford? Lovely place. I was born there.
Walter Bunce, shepherd
Mind the ewes, they're touchy after the shearing. Never you mind that they look so thin, it's only their wool's off.
Mr Arthur Fenn, yachtsman
Mind the bowsprit! She's a ten-rater, built her myself. Breeze is sou'westerly, she'll run beautifully today.
Do you bat or bowl? I bowl. Ask David's team about my yorkers, if they'll tell you.
Mr Edwin Marsh, warder
Welcome to the State Apartments. Mind the stair, it's old, and look up: those are King George the First's courtiers looking down at you, painted two hundred years ago.
Shh, she's only just gone off. Lovely afternoon for it. Have you seen the new statue down by the water? The children won't leave it alone.
Afternoon. Crossing? Wait for the bus to pass, then go smartly.
